---
title: "Pretesting a scale without real data"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5,
                      dpi = 96, out.width = "100%")
```

**Experimental.** Most people who write a new scale have no real data yet.
`synthetic_pretest()` is for that stage. It runs a standard item analysis on
synthetic respondents and flags items worth a second look. It also asks two
questions that stand in for real data: Do the flags hold across models,
temperatures, prompt wordings and persona sets? And do the synthetic answers
recover the structure you designed?

This is **pilot screening, not validation**. Language models answer more
tidily than people do (see the [benchmark article](benchmark.html)), so a
clean pretest does not show that a scale works in people. Items that fail
even with tidy respondents are the ones to rewrite first.

## The data

The tutorial treats two HEXACO traits, Honesty-Humility (H) and
Conscientiousness (C), as if they were a new 80-item scale. The six models in
`hexaco_llm` are the conditions, with three attempts each:

```{r}
library(synthcheck)

items <- hexaco_items[hexaco_items$trait %in% c("H", "C"), ]
synthetic <- hexaco_llm[hexaco_llm$country == "Canada" & hexaco_llm$attempt <= 3, ]
table(synthetic$model)
```

For your own scale, generate the data with `generate_synthetic()` or the app
(see [Generating synthetic respondents in R](generate.html)). The item table
needs `item` and `scale`, and `reverse` for reverse-keyed items. Those
columns are the structure the pretest checks.

## Run the pretest

```{r}
pt <- synthetic_pretest(synthetic, items, by = "model", irt = FALSE)
pt
```

Each row of the summary is one condition: How many items it flags, the mean
alpha over scales, the number of dimensions parallel analysis finds over all
items (next to the two scales designed), the share of items that relate most
to their own scale, and the share of reverse-keyed items whose key comes
through.

`irt = TRUE` (the default) also fits a graded response model per scale with
mirt and flags items with a slope below 0.5. It is the slowest step, so it is
off here.

## Which items are flagged, and by how many models?

An item is flagged when it barely varies (SD below 0.5, or 90% of the answers
in one category), when its keyed answers run against the rest of its scale,
when its item-rest correlation is below 0.3, when it relates more to another
scale than to its own, or when it correlates 0.85 or more with another item.
`thresholds` changes any of these.

```{r, fig.height = 7}
gg_pretest(pt, max_items = 25)
```

Red tiles are items with too little signal, blue tiles are near-duplicates,
and the label gives the number of models that flag the item. `agreement`
holds the same information as a table, most often flagged first:

```{r}
head(pt$agreement[, c("item", "scale", "flagged_in", "flags", "attempt_share")], 10)
```

`attempt_share` is the share of single attempts that flag the item. A flag
that comes and goes between attempts of the same model may be sampling noise.

Here most items are flagged by at least one model, and "Barely varies" and
"Near-duplicate" are the most common reasons. That is the tidy answering of
language models, not a property of 80 bad items. When this happens, start
with the items that most models agree on, and read "Weak link" and "Reverse
key not working" before the other flags.

## Do the conditions agree?

`stability` compares every pair of conditions: The rank correlation of their
item-rest correlations (`rho`) and the share of flagged items they have in
common (`jaccard`).

```{r}
pt$stability
```

On HEXACO the models agree only in part: Some pairs rank the items alike, and
others not at all. Low agreement is a finding too: It means a different model would have told
you to fix different items. The same comparison works for temperatures,
prompt wordings or persona sets. Give each run its own label and pass that
column as `by`, or several columns, as in `by = c("model", "wording")`. In
the app, "Or several temperatures" in the Models tab adds one model per
temperature.

## Does the designed structure come back?

```{r}
pt$summary[, c("condition", "scales", "n_factors", "own_scale", "reverse_ok")]
gg_pretest(pt, "scales")
```

Almost every item relates most to the scale it was written for, and the
reverse keys come through. Parallel analysis finds more dimensions than the
two scales, because each HEXACO trait has four facets; the real data below
give more than two as well. The scale plot shows
the tidy answers again: Alpha is 0.95 or more for many models, higher than
real people give.

## Plain language

```{r}
summarise_pretest(pt)
```

## How well do the flags match real people?

The HEXACO data come with real responses, so this tutorial can check what the
pretest would have found in people. `synthetic_pretest()` works on any data:

```{r}
real <- hexaco_real[hexaco_real$country == "Canada", ]
pr <- synthetic_pretest(real, items, by = NULL, irt = FALSE)
real_flags <- pr$items[pr$items$weak | pr$items$key, c("item", "item_rest", "flags")]
real_flags
```

How many of the six models flag these items as weak or running against their
scale?

```{r}
it <- as.data.frame(pt$items)
it$weak_or_key <- it$weak | it$key
n_models <- tapply(it$weak_or_key, it$item, sum)
data.frame(item = real_flags$item, models = n_models[real_flags$item])
```

And how closely do the item-rest correlations of each model follow the real
ones (rank correlation)?

```{r}
real_ir <- setNames(pr$items$item_rest, pr$items$item)
sapply(split(it, it$condition), function(d)
  round(cor(d$item_rest, real_ir[d$item], method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"), 2))
```

The models catch some of the items that are weak in people, and they agree
with real people on the ranking of the items only in part. That is why the
pretest is screening: It points at items to read again, and a field test
still decides.

## In the app

On the About tab of the app, answer **No, not yet** to the first question.
The fourth tab is then **Pretest**: Choose the synthetic data, what to
compare the flags across and click **Run the pretest**. The **Interviews**
tab (5) that follows runs cognitive interviews on the flagged items, as in
[the cognitive interviews tutorial](cognitive-interviews.html). See
[the tour of the app](app-tour.html#pretest-without-real-data).

## Later: Real data

The pretest keeps the item table in `pt$settings$items`. Once real responses
come in, the same synthetic data go straight into the benchmark, and the app
lets you switch the first question to "Yes, I have real data":

```{r, eval = FALSE}
real <- read.csv("my_real_data.csv")
authenticity_benchmark(as_synthetic_list(synthetic), real, pt$settings$items)
```
